en: The Eight Verses in Praise of the Feet of the Blessed Śrīmacchaṅkara.

He whose gait is worthy of the renowned supreme swan, who sports in the playground of the Vedas, and who delights in his own true abode that transcends the three worlds—he is indeed like Brahmā in this matter; yet I consider the meaning of the root *bṛh* (to expand) here to be direct, non-figurative, and absolute. The entire triple world is measured by him with but a single foot through his splendor; he is that pure *sattva* which persists even through the states of creation, maintenance, and dissolution.

Transcending the ten states (*daśākāra*), delighting in his own majesty through detachment, the Veda then declares him to be that supreme state of Viṣṇu. (2) With no attachment to beings anywhere, wandering without a vehicle, having no contact with prosperity, nor even acquaintance with those who enjoy worldly pleasures—even so, the end of the Veda describes him as the fourth state (*turīya*), beyond duality, auspicious, and exceedingly peaceful, following the burning of Tripura. (3)
There is no golden dharma, no inclination toward the fruits of human effort, nor indeed a royal chariot flashing day and night with enemies;
yet, since the eight cities have been utterly conquered, how could the collection of conclusions not proclaim that Supreme Śiva?

Avoiding from afar the terrible and irresistible rainy season of miserable rebirths—dense with the clouds of evil deeds and the downpours of suffering—the noble-minded one sports in the beautiful lake of the True Mind. There he dwells as the crest-jewel of the swan-flock, consuming the sprouts of the lotus-stalks that are the fame of the arrogant scholars who are his fierce adversaries.

Milk is Brahman and the world is water; these two, having come together in union, were difficult to distinguish from one another for a very long time, until he who has perfectly separated them—this supreme Swan, the foremost leader of the twice-born, purifies the intellect that has reached the surging waves of desire for every particular excellence. That sage named Śrī Śaṅkara, who distinguishes the real from the unreal when they are blended together like milk and water—a task difficult for all but the wise to comprehend.
Let this swan be supreme; however, we consider all those who remain here powerless to be merely crows, solely intent on devouring the fruits of the *jumbha* and *nimba* trees.
He who straightens his vision, which has been dimmed by external darkness, does not turn toward a fondness for the lotus (or women), but cultivates unimpeded friendship;
he destroys the suffering of the circle of friends and dispels the distress of the world for its benefit—this swan repeatedly reveals the meaning that is to be known by the great.
Thus ends the *Śrīmacchaṅkarabhagavaccaraṇastutyaṣṭaka* composed by the venerable sage Vidyāraṇya.
